newsitem.title: USA: Sherwin-Williams sees Minwax accretive in'98.
newsitem.headline: Sherwin-Williams sees Minwax accretive in'98.

text.p: Sherwin-Williams Co said Friday it expects its $830 million acquisition of Thompson Minwax Holding Corp to help 1998 earnings if completed by 1996 yearend as planned.
For 1997, the paint company said it expects its existing businesses to offset the deal's dilutive effect on earnings. The stock closed off 3/4 at 56 on the New York Stock Exchange.
"If we close (the deal) at the end of 1996, we would expect it to be accretive to earnings in 1998," vice president of corporate planning/development Conway Ivy said.
In a telephone interview, he said that in 1997, the paint and coatings maker expects its existing businesses to offset any dilutive effect of the acquisition.

As reported earlier, the Cleveland-based company said it plans to purchase Thompson Minwax from Forstmann Little & Co affiliates for cash. The New Jersey company's products, mainly for wood, include Minwax stains and varnishes, Thompson's exterior sealers and Formby's, Red Devil and Ronseal products.
Sherwin-Williams said Thompson Minwax has annual sales of about $375 million.
In 1995 Sherwin-Williams earned $200.7 million, or $2.34 a share, on net sales of $3.27 billion. Its brands include Dutch Boy, Pratt & Lambert, Martin-Senour and Krylon.
Ivy said Sherwin-Williams will finance the purchase price through debt and is considering various debt instruments.
He said the company ended the third quarter with about $359 million in debt.

As reported earlier, Standard & Poor's said after the acquisition announcement that it may cut Sherwin-Williams debt ratings. The rating agency placed its single-A-plus senior unsecured debt and corporate credit ratings and its A-1 commercial paper rating on CreditWatch with negative implications.

The Cleveland-based company has made about one acquisition a month in 1996 and made several in 1995. The $400 million acquisition of Pratt & Lambert United Inc, completed in January, was previously its largest. In 1995, Sherwin-Williams was outbid by Imperial Chemical Industries Plc for Grow Group, a coatings company.
Ivy said acquisitions are shifting Sherwin-Williams' business mix. Its retail store business has accounted for about two-thirds of overall revenues in recent years.
"Our stores business has been growing very well this year," he said. But as the coatings segment grows through acquisitions, it will likely account for about half of revenues, he said.
He said it is unlikely that the company will undertake any additional large acquisitions or repurchase stock in the near future due to the debt it will undertake for Thompson Minwax.
But he said the board of directors traditionally increases the shareholder dividend in February.
McDonald & Co analyst Justin Maurer said the Thompson Minwax deal is a good move.
Maurer agreed it should not have much negative effect on 1997 earnings, partly due to Pratt & Lambert which will begin to help earnings in 1997 after a neutral effect in 1996.
Maurer said he may lower his 1997 earnings estimate of $3.05 a share to $3.00 but said the company's fundamentals remain strong. He rates the stock a hold due to its price.
The deal will bring to Sherwin-Williams leading brands of interior stain and exterior protective sealer, which are categories where the company is under-represented, Maurer said.
He said the stock price decline may have been because "people may think it's a little too expensive."
-- Cleveland Newsdesk, 216-579-0077
